Many still design a corporate website as a storefront. But if supplier comparison is increasingly performed by AI agents, that framework is no longer sufficient.

The website starts to function as a verifiable representation of the business.

What does this change at the architecture level?

First, you need a single canonical source of truth. The human-facing page and the machine layer should not exist separately. Price, terms, availability, constraints, and the composition of the service are described once and then projected in both directions.

Second, it is important to distinguish between two classes of entities: comparable facts and trusted claims. The former are provided as a clean machine-readable model. The latter require a separate verification mechanism: identity, qualifications, provenance, guarantees, and the boundaries of responsibility.

Third, agent-readiness is not the same as a new decorative add-on. Semantic HTML, JSON-LD, stable structure, accessibility, and avoiding excessive dependence on JS are not cosmetics, but the basic discipline of a well-built web.

And finally: the human layer is not going anywhere. It remains wherever an action becomes binding, financially significant, or irreversible.

In the article, I examine this model not as a prediction of interfaces, but as a set of engineering invariants that will survive protocol changes.
